misconceptions.description: Assuming that because an AI tool makes a teaching task faster it has improved student learning
misconceptions.trigger: teacher justifies adopting a tool only by time saved on grading, planning, or feedback
misconceptions.feedback: Separate the labor change from the learning change. Name the specific learning activity the tool improves and the evidence you would inspect, not just the minutes saved.

misconceptions.description: Believing an AI tool is a neutral instrument whose effects depend only on how the teacher uses it
misconceptions.trigger: teacher dismisses equity or data concerns by saying the tool is just a tool
misconceptions.feedback: A tool carries design assumptions about who it serves and what data it collects. Name one assumption built into this tool and how it shifts who benefits in your classroom.

misconceptions.description: Choosing an AI tool because it is new or engaging rather than because it serves a named instructional purpose
misconceptions.trigger: teacher cannot state the learning goal the tool serves but cites student excitement
misconceptions.feedback: Write the instructional purpose first, then ask whether this tool serves it better than your current approach. Excitement is not the purpose.

misconceptions.description: Adopting AI for a task without noticing what valuable practice or judgment it removes from students
misconceptions.trigger: teacher adds an AI step without naming the student thinking it replaces
misconceptions.feedback: For every task AI takes over, name the cognitive work students no longer do, then decide whether that work was the point of the lesson.
